method.value: LTE slab grid in column density and excitation temperature; optimize emitting area at each point.

For each grid point, the LTE spectrum of SO$_2$ was calculated at a spectral resolving power of $R=3500$ and the best-fitting emitting area was computed by minimizing the $\chi^2$ (cite: Grant2023).

method.value: Compare ALMA SO2 molecule count with warm H2; assess hot-core and shock origins using abundance, emission size, morphology and linewidth.

evidence.quote: The total number of SO$_2$ molecules derived from the emission of the vibrational ground state in the ALMA data can be directly compared to H$_2$.
Based on the size of the emitting area ($\sim100$ au in radius) and the small line width of the SO$_2$ lines ($\sim3.5$ km s$^{-1}$) in the ALMA data, a hot core origin is suggested

claims.hypothesis: MIRI ν3 emission can be explained by LTE excitation.
claims.experiment: Compare MIRI LTE molecule counts and emitting extent with ALMA and predict the ν2 band.
claims.result: MIRI LTE requires ∼2×10^4 more molecules; the ν3-based LTE model predicts undetected ν2 emission.
claims.finding: The MIR ν3 emission is not in LTE.

evidence.quote: the total number of molecules can be constrained and is predicted by LTE models of the MIRI-MRS data to be a factor of $\sim2\times10^4$ higher than derived from the ALMA data.
No obvious SO$_2$ emission features are present in the data whereas the best-fit $\nu_3$ LTE model clearly predicts that we should have seen the SO$_2$ at these wavelengths.
The $\nu_3$ asymmetric stretching mode of SO$_2$ detected around 7.35 $\mu$m with MIRI is not in LTE

claims.hypothesis: Infrared pumping explains the enhanced ν3 population.
claims.experiment: Estimate Tvib from the MIRI/ALMA discrepancy and compare with the infrared continuum brightness temperature.
claims.finding: The infrared radiation field sets the ν3 vibrational temperature.

evidence.quote: results in $T_{\rm vib} \sim 200$ K
this results in $T_{\rm IR} \sim 180$ K.
strongly suggests that the vibrational temperature of the $\nu_3$ band of SO$_2$ is indeed set by the infrared radiation field of the protostar rather than by collisions.

claims.hypothesis: MIRI and ALMA probe the same SO2 gas.
claims.experiment: Compare rotational temperatures and spatial extents.
claims.result: 92±8 K from MIRI versus 104±5 K from ALMA; similar emission extents.
claims.finding: Both facilities likely trace the same molecular gas.

evidence.quote: A rotational temperature of $92\pm8$ K is derived from the $\nu_3$ lines.

This is in good agreement with the rotational temperature derived from pure rotational lines in the vibrational ground state (i.e., $\nu$=0) with ALMA ($104\pm5$ K) which are extended over similar scales.
The similarity in rotational temperatures suggests that MIRI-MRS and ALMA are in fact still tracing the same molecular gas.

claims.hypothesis: SO2 originates from hot-core ice sublimation rather than an accretion shock.
claims.experiment: Compare abundance, emission extent, morphology and linewidth with the proposed origins.
claims.result: Abundance 1.0±0.3×10^-8 is consistent with both origins; ∼100 au radius and ∼3.5 km s^-1 linewidth favor a hot core.
claims.finding: A hot core is the most likely origin, while abundance alone does not distinguish it from shocks.

evidence.quote: the abundance of gaseous SO$_2$ is estimated to be $1.0\pm0.3\times10^{-8}$ with respect to H$_2$, which is consistent with both a hot core and accretion shock origin.
Based on the size of the emitting area ($\sim100$ au in radius) and the small line width of the SO$_2$ lines ($\sim3.5$ km s$^{-1}$) in the ALMA data, a hot core origin is suggested
A hot core origin is therefore a more likely explanation for the gaseous SO$_2$.

limitations_admitted.value: A larger sample is needed to test luminosity dependence of MIR SO2 emission.

referee_caveats_inferred: The ALMA molecule count is inconsistent between sections: 1.6±0.2×10^47 versus 1.8±0.2×10^47.
Only two relatively unblended SO2 transitions and one 34SO2 transition constrain the ALMA fit.
The text calls τ∼0.1 marginally optically thick; the resulting column–area constraint deserves direct verification.
The abundance depends on assumed dust temperature, opacity, gas-to-dust ratio and density-profile scaling.
The printed dust-opacity units need clarification before implementing the mass equation.
The pumping calculation is an approximate consistency test rather than a full non-LTE fit.
The hot-core interpretation is favored but does not uniquely exclude weak accretion shocks.
